clips.caption:
Charlie Munger said a great investor needs temperament more than skill - handling huge wins without getting overexcited, and real losses without falling apart.

Former Navy SEAL Garrett Unclebock says the same trait decides who makes it through SEAL training: equanimity. You don't panic when you're getting shot at, so you can keep doing the job.

His now-wife once called him crying on the highway with a flat tire. His answer: 'No amount of tears is going to change that flat tire.' Not cold - panic wasn't going to fix anything, and calm would get her home faster.

The skill isn't staying happy. It's staying steady.

clips.end_words: I can make the next one
clips.caption:
Navy SEAL instructors tell every class on day one: 'SEALs aren't made. SEALs show up to be trained.' Former SEAL Garrett Unclebock says the program isn't testing fitness - it's testing one specific trait.

Confidence is 'I made a hundred free throws, I know I can make another one.' That's easy. It only shows up after success.

Resilience is the opposite: 'I've missed a hundred free throws in a row, but I know I can make the next one.' That's the trait that actually gets people through.

Which one are you actually running on right now?

#kevintrudeau #mindset #resilience #navyseal #successmindset #discipline

Former Navy SEAL Garrett Unclebock draws a hard line between two kinds of strong men.

Barbarians are strong and tough - you've met plenty of them in business, guys with power who use it to take. Warriors are also strong. The difference is who it's for.

His own words on why he wanted to be a SEAL: not to prove how strong he was, but because there were people who couldn't do that job, and he could do it for them.

That same shift - from strength that's about you to strength that's for someone else - is what he says actually grows a man into the best version of himself.

Which one are you building toward?

clips.end_words: priority that you give to the facts
clips.caption:
Mike Siegel is a 10-time world champion pool player, one of the greatest to ever pick up a cue.

Former Navy SEAL Garrett Unclebock once reminded him of a tournament where his opponent, Efren Reyes, hit an impossible shot and beat him. Mike's answer: 'I don't remember that.' What he does remember in perfect detail is coming back from 9-0 down against Johnny Archer to win 11-9.

Same man, same career, two very different sets of facts to choose from.

His point: the facts are the facts, but the story is the order and priority you give them. The losses you replay, and the comebacks you forget, are both a choice.

clips.end_words: would never have given their life for
clips.caption:
Former Navy SEAL Garrett Unclebock talks about his friend Charlie Keating, who died in May 2016 with a smile on his face.

It wasn't the $400,000 death benefit his wife would receive. It wasn't about money at all. He died smiling because he'd given his life to something he actually believed was worth it.

Unclebock's point: everyone dies for something. Most people just do it slowly, over decades, for something they would never have actually chosen to die for in an instant.

What are you spending your life on right now - something worth that, or just something that's there?

#kevintrudeau #mindset #purpose #navyseal #success #motivation

Most people don't know Tesla's actual vision statement. It says nothing about cars: 'to accelerate the world's transition to renewable energy.'

Former Navy SEAL Garrett Unclebock uses it to explain vision versus mission. The vision is advancing human civilization - the thing worth building a life around.

The mission is just the clear target that serves it: 'make the most compelling electric car of the 21st century.' Make it cool, people buy it, that funds the battery technology the real vision needed all along.

Most people chase the mission and never define the vision it's supposed to serve.
